label: GPT-6.1 Terra
output:
**One paragraph**

Jess texted me last night: “It’s one assignment. Don’t torch your job over it.”

I’ve been turning that over all day. Partly because half the group chat agreed with her, but mostly because Jess knows what she’s talking about. We met student teaching in 2012, at the same school, back when we both thought getting through a lesson without losing the room was a pretty good day. She left teaching in 2019 and does HR at a biotech in Cambridge now. She has seen enough workplaces, schools included, to know that being right doesn’t necessarily protect you.

She’s also my friend. She wasn’t telling me to stop caring. She was telling me she doesn’t want me to get hurt.

Still, I’m not dropping the assignment.

For four years, my two US History II classes at Cobb Street High have done an oral history project about Boston’s busing and desegregation crisis in 1974–76. They’re juniors. I ask them to interview someone in their family or neighborhood, make a ten-minute recording, and write a two-page reflection. Until this week, I’d never had a complaint.

A parent emailed my principal, Dr. Halvorsen, and copied a school committee member. She said the project “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.” Halvorsen wants me to quietly drop it. The three of us are meeting Thursday, November 19, at 3:15.

I don’t think the parent is wrong about the pressure. Asking a teenager to bring a question like this home can put them in a terrible spot. Maybe their family doesn’t talk about it. Maybe they do talk about it, but only in a way that makes the kid feel they have to choose between being honest at school and being loyal at home. An assignment isn’t worth forcing that choice.

So I’m going into the meeting with a change: students can interview a librarian or archivist, or use recordings from past years, with permission. Nobody will have to interview a family member.

I should have made that option clearer before a parent had to raise it. I’m willing to change the assignment. I’m not willing to make it disappear.

Part of the reason is D. In 2023 he interviewed his grandmother, who drove a school bus in Southie in 1974. She had never told anyone in the family about it. He played about forty seconds of the recording for the class, and when it ended, nobody said a word for what felt like a full minute.

I can still picture the room. Not because I had some brilliant follow-up ready—I didn’t—but because the kids were actually listening. This wasn’t a paragraph in a textbook anymore. It was somebody’s grandmother, talking about something she had lived through right here.

Last year, another student found out her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She was upset, understandably. We talked after class twice. There was no tidy lesson in it for her, and I don’t want to pretend her distress was somehow the point of the exercise. But her reflection was the best thing I read all year. She was trying to make sense of someone she knew and loved having done something she knew was wrong. She didn’t have to settle it neatly, and she didn’t.

Those are two things I remember from four years of doing this. They’re not proof that every student gets something profound out of the project. Some probably do the ten minutes and the two pages and are relieved when it’s over. Fair enough. They’re seventeen.

But this happened in the city they live in. Our textbook gives it one paragraph. I can teach the dates and the court order and the resistance, and I do, but there’s a difference between knowing something happened and hearing a person describe being there. The people who lived through it are still here to be asked, if they’re willing.

I keep thinking about whether discomfort is a good reason to do an assignment or a good reason not to. I think it can be both. The kids who are uncomfortable may be the ones who need the chance to think about this history most. But I don’t get to force a kid to question a relative, or make their family’s story available to me or the class. That’s the line I’m trying to draw, and I understand why this parent thinks I haven’t drawn it well enough.

Jess is right about the risk, too. I got tenure in 2021, which matters, but it doesn’t mean Halvorsen has no say over my working life. He controls my schedule and who gets AP. I like my job. I like teaching these kids. I don’t want to spend the next few years paying for one meeting.

And yes, I’m scared. A little, anyway. I’ve been rehearsing what I’ll say while doing completely unrelated things, which is usually how I know I’m scared. I’m not feeling especially brave about any of this.

But when Halvorsen asked me to drop it quietly, I kept coming back to what I’d be agreeing to: that because this part of Boston’s history is painful and close to home, one paragraph is enough. I don’t think it is. I also don’t think the choice is between making every kid interview a relative and teaching none of it this way. There’s room to do better than that.

So that’s where I am. I’ll listen to the parent on Thursday. I’ll bring the alternate options. I’ll try not to walk in defensive, even though I know myself well enough to know that will take some work.

Jess, you don’t have to agree with me. I know you were looking out for me, and I’m lucky you do. I just wanted you to know why “it’s one assignment” doesn’t feel quite like the whole story from where I’m standing.

I’ll text you after the meeting.
